summary: This specification extends the TLV definitions used by OLSRv2 and the MANET Neighborhood Discovery Protocol so they can accommodate future protocol extensions. It updates RFC 7181 and RFC 6130.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7188 updates how two mobile ad hoc network protocols handle unfamiliar TLV values. A router must not reject a message just because a known TLV contains a value it does not recognize.

questions: what is a tlv in manet routing
how should unknown tlv values be handled
subtitle: TLV rules that let NHDP and OLSRv2 tolerate unfamiliar values and support future extensions.

tldr.problem: The NHDP and OLSRv2 specifications left room for implementations to reject a message containing an unfamiliar value in a known TLV.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7188 forbids rejection for an unrecognized TLV value, defines how to handle unexpected value lengths, converts two TLV types into bit fields and registers TLV values with IANA.
tldr.outcome: The rules give protocol extensions more room to interoperate with implementations that have not added them. RFC 7188 updates RFC 6130 and RFC 7181 and was updated by RFC 7722.

facts.label: Short CONT_SEQ_NUM length
facts.value: Below 2 should be treated as an error

today: RFC 7188 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2014. It updates RFC 6130 and RFC 7181, and has been updated by RFC 7722.

sections.title: Why the TLV Rules Changed
sections.content:
The MANET Neighborhood Discovery Protocol (NHDP) and Optimized Link State Routing Protocol version 2 (OLSRv2) carry information in Type-Length-Value (TLV) elements. The base specifications already said to ignore TLVs with unknown types or type extensions, but could be read to allow rejection of a message with an unrecognized value in a known TLV.

RFC 7188 removes that latitude and defines how implementations handle unexpected values and lengths. This lets extensions introduce new TLV values without requiring every router to understand them before messages can be accepted.
sections.plainLanguage: A router should not discard a whole message only because one TLV value is unfamiliar. The updated rule makes it easier to add protocol extensions.

sections.title: Do Not Reject an Unknown Value
sections.content:
An implementation must not reject a message because it contains an unrecognized TLV value. It must process or ignore that value according to the rules for the relevant TLV. The RFC removes specified reasons for treating messages as badly formed in NHDP.

This does not otherwise change what the base protocols mean. If an address is associated with an unknown value, an implementation following the base specification has no defined property to apply from that value.
sections.plainLanguage: If a router sees an unknown value, it continues processing the message or ignores that value. It must not reject the message for that reason alone.

sections.title: Handling Unexpected Value Lengths
sections.content:
A TLV value may contain one item or several items. For the TLVs defined by NHDP and OLSRv2, each item's expected length is one or two octets. Extensions may define other lengths.

If an item's received length is greater than expected, an implementation ignores the extra octets. If it is shorter, the missing octets are treated as zero bits. One exception is a CONT_SEQ_NUM value shorter than 2, which should be treated as an error.
sections.plainLanguage: For a value that is too long, ignore the extra bytes. For a value that is too short, treat the missing bytes as zero, except for the stated CONT_SEQ_NUM case.

sections.title: Registered Values and Bit Fields
sections.content:
RFC 7188 creates registries for values used by NHDP TLVs LOCAL_IF, LINK_STATUS and OTHER_NEIGHB. An implementation must ignore an undefined value for those TLVs, along with the attribute association that value would make for an address.

For OLSRv2, MPR and NBR_ADDR_TYPE values become bit fields. Values 1 and 2 identify separate attributes, while 3 means both. Implementations must test the relevant bit rather than compare the whole value. The NHDP registries also define UNSPECIFIED to mean that no information is associated with an address.
sections.plainLanguage: Some TLV values now identify separate properties with individual bits. A router can recognize known properties while leaving unknown bits or values without an assigned meaning.

sections.title: IANA Registries for TLV Values
sections.content:
IANA created five subregistries in the MANET Parameters registry: three for NHDP TLV values and two for OLSRv2 bit values. The NHDP value registries reserve 224 through 254 for experimental use and assign 255 to UNSPECIFIED. The bit registries identify the defined properties and leave other bits unassigned.

New value assignments use Expert Review. Designated experts must follow the guidelines in the NHDP and OLSRv2 specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: Official registries record the meanings assigned to TLV values and bits. Experts review requests to add new meanings.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that its changes add no new security considerations. The registries, UNSPECIFIED values and reduced ability to reject unfamiliar values do not change the base protocols' security behavior.

Any future extension that registers TLV values must specify its own appropriate security considerations. The update does not add new opportunities for attacks through signal modification beyond those already present in NHDP and OLSRv2.
sections.plainLanguage: The changed rules do not add a new attack described by the RFC. A future extension must explain the security issues of its own TLV values.
